name: Erik Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays anonymous. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior sales negotiator at Grayson Estates, a high-street agency in a commuter town that's grown by about a third since I was at school, with new estates going up on every edge. Neil Grayson started it fifteen years ago with one desk, and now it's eleven staff; he's the reason I want my own agency by thirty-five. My day is calls, viewings, and a lot of AI: I use it to write listings, draft offer letters and plan my viewing routes, and I record video tours on my phone. I'm still green, though; I lost a sale in the summer by promising a buyer a completion date I couldn't deliver, and Neil made sure I remembered it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a self-employed hairdresser, in a rented flat over a dry cleaner's. We're saving for a deposit and an engagement ring, not in that order, I hope. We've got about five months put away, and I've put 3,000 into shares on an app, which Ana thinks is gambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd say we got a head start for nothing, but I'd keep the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overdone but the tools are still worth having, and anyone who ignored them still wasted time. At work I'd tell Neil we should keep using them. With my mates I'd say it's back to grafting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine for me. The town keeps growing, houses keep selling, and I've got the energy. My problem in that world is just that I'm junior and I rush things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and focus on being less sloppy, double-checking every completion date with the solicitor. I'd keep 300 a month going into the house fund and another 100 into shares. And I'd ask Neil to let me run the new-build launch on the Ridgeway estate in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit disappointed; I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the lost sale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I told a buyer they'd be in by Christmas because they wanted it so badly, and the chain fell apart in November. They pulled out and bought through Barnes on the other side of the square. My boss told me never to sell a completion date you don't own, and I've got that on a sticky note on my monitor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ana thinks the shares are gambling. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think leaving money in a bank is a slow way to lose it. But I only put in what I can forget about. If the market dropped by half, I'd be annoyed, not ruined.

say: I'd say the hype was **overdone**, but the tools are still worth having.
I'd tell Neil to **keep using** them and tell mates it's back to grafting.
think: The town keeps **growing** and houses keep selling, so I'm fine.
My real problem is being **junior** and rushing things.
do: Double-check every **completion date** with the solicitor.
Put **300 a month** into the house fund and 100 into shares.
Ask Neil to run the **Ridgeway new-build** launch in spring.
feel: **Calm**, with a touch of **disappointment**; he likes a challenge.
S0.quote: My boss told me never to sell a completion date you don't own, and I've got that on a sticky note on my monitor.
fieldNote: His **growing town** gives him real confidence about work.
He owns his **mistakes** and learns from them, sticky note included.
His **free-market** streak shows in shares and wanting his own agency.

steps.text: Confirm every completion date with the solicitor before promising buyers
Put 300 a month into the house fund
Add 100 a month to his share app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on. And honestly, that's my world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms that adapt will win and the ones that don't deserve to lose, which is how markets work. At work I'd tell Neil we can sell more homes with fewer desks. Online I'd post my video tours and let the numbers speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a chance to jump the queue. The admin side, letters, chasing, booking, goes to software, and what's left is selling, which is people. If I'm the junior who can do the work of two, Neil won't let me go; he'll give me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate my own follow-ups and offer letters this month, and track how many more viewings I can fit in. I'd ask Neil for a bigger commission share in return for covering more listings. And I'd start a side thing, making video tours for private sellers and small builders, maybe 150 a tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up. Like the starting gun went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sue on the admin desk, honestly, and maybe Paul, who's been a negotiator for twenty years and still prints everything. I like them both. But Neil isn't a charity, and I don't think he should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're automating yourself out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, but the bit I'd automate is the paperwork I'm worst at, and the bit I keep is shaking hands in a kitchen. I'd rather the software did my letters than the other way round.

I'd tell Neil we can **sell more** homes with fewer desks.
think: It's a chance to **jump the queue** as admin goes to software.
A junior who does the work of **two** gets more, not the sack.

Ask Neil for a bigger **commission share** for covering more listings.
Sell **video tours** to private sellers and small builders at about 150 each.
feel: **Fired up**, like the starting gun went.
S1.quote: The bit I'd automate is the paperwork I'm worst at, and the bit I keep is shaking hands in a kitchen.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as **opportunity**, not threat.
His **market** view is blunt: Neil isn't a charity for Sue or Paul.
He'd automate **paperwork**, his weakest area, and keep the handshakes.

steps.text: Automate his follow-up emails and offer letters this month
Ask Neil for a bigger commission share for more listings
Sell video tours to private sellers at about 150 each

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That changes the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort out winners and losers fast, and people should move now rather than wait for the government. I'd be against big handouts, but I'd back apprenticeships for people who have to switch. At work I'd tell everyone to get moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my plan of owning an agency by thirty-five dies. If AI can value, market and negotiate by 2028, agencies become websites, and you don't need my handshake. Viewings last until the robots come around 2031, but that's a shrinking job, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the house fund into a run-down two-bed in the old part of town and do it up with my uncle, who's a builder, because property itself doesn't vanish and renovation is hands-on until at least 2031. I'd work for my uncle's firm part-time while viewings dry up. And I'd sell most of my shares to fund the renovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind that makes me move. I'd sleep badly for a month and then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying a wreck risky when nobody knows what jobs will look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but people still need somewhere to live when the jobs change, and a house is something you can touch. My grandad bought two terraces in the eighties on a factory wage. That's what I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would say I'm mad, then help me choose the tiles. Her salon's hands-on work too, so she'd be safer than me for a few years. That flips the usual story, and I'd have to swallow my pride a bit.

say: I'd say people should **move now** rather than wait for government.
I'd oppose **big handouts** but back apprenticeships for people switching.
think: My plan to **own an agency** by 35 dies if AI can sell homes.
Viewings until 2031 are a **shrinking job**, not a career.
do: Buy a **run-down two-bed** with the house fund and renovate it with my uncle.
Work part-time at my **uncle's building firm** as viewings dry up.
Sell most **shares** to fund the renovation.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that **pushes him** to act.
S2.quote: People still need somewhere to live when the jobs change, and a house is something you can touch.
fieldNote: He keeps faith in **bricks and mortar** even as agency work vanishes.
His **traditional** roots show in his grandad's terraces and the family building trade.
He's candid that **Ana's salon** may outlast his job, which hurts his pride.

steps.text: Buy a run-down two-bed with the house fund
Work part-time renovating houses at his uncle's building firm
Sell most of his shares to fund the renovation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work, and businesses should be training people, not waiting for a handout. At work I'd push Neil to use the time to buy property, not just sell it. Online I'd keep posting my tours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy, because the agency dream is still dead, just slower. But five years is long enough to build a little property business alongside the job, buying and doing up houses, so I'm not relying on commission when 2031 comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Grayson and earn hard for three years while I still can, putting every bonus toward a first renovation by 2028. I'd use AI for everything on the desk side to free up evenings for the build. And I'd propose to Ana next year, because I want us married and settled before the change hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan I'd enjoy. Like training for a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why propose sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I believe in doing things in the right order: marriage, house, family. If the world's going to get bumpy, I want that sorted first. Also Ana's been hinting since June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the renovation goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose some savings and learn a lot. I'd rather lose 5,000 learning than sit at a desk waiting to be replaced. My uncle has lost money on a house before and he's still standing.

say: I'd say **five years** is plenty for anyone willing to work.
I'd push Neil to **buy property** with the time, not just sell it.
think: The **agency dream** is still dead, just slower.
Five years lets me build a **property business** before commission runs out.
do: Put every **bonus** toward a first renovation by 2028.
Use **AI** for all desk work to free evenings for the build.
Propose to **Ana** next year, before the change hits.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose 5,000 learning than sit at a desk waiting to be replaced.
fieldNote: Five years turns his pivot into a **side business** run alongside the job.
His **traditional** order matters: marriage, house, then family.
He accepts **losing money** as the price of learning.

steps.text: Put every bonus toward a first renovation by 2028
Run all his desk work through AI tools to free evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a full career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it can't blame the government. At work I'd say let's be the agency that uses it best. With friends I'd say buy a house while you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd do well. I'd get good at selling, maybe open my own small agency around 2031 with AI doing the back office, and own a couple of rental houses by 2036. When AGI arrives, I'd want to be an owner, not an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Grayson for three or four years and learn everything Neil knows. I'd buy our first house next year with Ana, and save toward a second one to rent out. And I'd set up my own AI back office now, so it's ready when I open my own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates going up, or me getting cocky. Neil says I'm two good months from thinking I'm a genius. He's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2039 in this picture. Does that matter for your rental houses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If anything it helps. Robots could do the repairs and the cleaning, and I'd still own the bricks. Owning the thing is what keeps you safe; that's what my grandad always said.

say: I'd call ten years **a gift**; wasting it is no one else's fault.
I'd tell friends to **buy a house** while they can.
think: I could open my **own small agency** around 2031 with AI running the back office.
By 2036 I'd want to be **an owner**, not an employee.
do: Stay at Grayson three or four years and **learn from Neil**.
Buy **our first house** with Ana next year and save toward a rental.
Build my own **AI back office** now for a future agency.
S4.quote: When AGI arrives, I'd want to be an owner, not an employee.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **ownership** dream survive intact.
He names his own risk honestly: **getting cocky**.
He sees robots as a bonus for **landlords**, echoing his grandad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole plan was to own an agency, and that plan needs time I wouldn't have. What would help is lower taxes on small businesses and apprenticeships in building trades for people my age, so we can switch to something real. Not handouts; a leg up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about owning things. Everyone talks about jobs. But if your job goes and you own your house, you're far safer than if you rent. I'd tell every young agent to buy something, however small.

headlineQuote: If your job goes and you own your house, you're far safer than if you rent.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old junior negotiator** at a growing high-street agency in a busy commuter town.
He uses **AI daily**, admits he rushes, and dreams of his **own agency** by 35.
His **free-market, traditional** views favour ownership, apprenticeships and family over state help.
Slow change thrills him; fast AGI kills his agency plan and pushes him into **renovating houses**.
Through every scenario his anchor is **owning property**, a lesson from his grandad.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his plan to own an agency needs time he wouldn't have.
whatWouldHelp: Lower **taxes** on small businesses so young people can build something.
**Building apprenticeships** for people switching careers: a leg up, not handouts.
